methodological_rigor.justification: This single-center retrospective study of 150 patients compares PAROS AI (biparametric MRI) against an expert radiologist (multiparametric MRI) using histopathology as reference standard. McNemar's test for sensitivity/specificity comparison and Pearson/Wilcoxon correlation for measurement agreement are appropriate. Key limitations include: the AI was evaluated on biparametric input while the radiologist used multiparametric sequences (unequal comparison); single expert reader prevents inter-reader analysis; high csPCa prevalence (63.3%) and few PI-RADS 1-2 patients from biopsy-required inclusion criteria inflate sensitivity estimates and limit generalizability to screening populations.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a retrospective single-center diagnostic accuracy study (LoE 4). The comparison of AI-assisted versus expert radiologist prostate MRI interpretation addresses a clinically relevant question given the shortage of experienced radiologists globally. Demonstrated comparable sensitivity/specificity, excellent NLRs for rule-out, and potential utility in supporting less-experienced readers have direct practice implications. However, the single-center design with enriched high-risk population and a pre-commercial trial version of PAROS limits immediate clinical applicability.

reporting_quality.justification: The study follows diagnostic accuracy reporting conventions consistent with STARD: eligibility criteria, index test, reference standard, and statistical measures (sensitivity, specificity, PLR, NLR with CIs) are clearly described at two PI-RADS thresholds. The biparametric vs. multiparametric comparison limitation is transparently acknowledged. No public data deposit is mentioned. The important disclosure that a pre-commercial trial version (not the current marketed version) was used is appropriately stated and its implications discussed.

novelty_literature.justification: Multiple AI tools for prostate MRI (Quantib, aPRIL, PI-CAI models) have been previously evaluated against radiologists, so this study contributes incremental evidence for one specific commercial tool. The explicit biparametric vs. multiparametric comparison framing and the measurement calibration findings (AI underestimates prostate volume by 5.6 mL, affecting PSA density) are clinically useful novel observations. The study adds to but does not transform the existing literature on AI-assisted prostate MRI.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written and well-organized with a logical progression. Limitations are comprehensively and transparently enumerated, including the biparametric comparison issue, single expert reader, enriched population, and pre-commercial software version. The discussion thoughtfully addresses clinical integration scenarios (specialized centers vs. resource-limited settings) and PSA density calibration implications. Some minor redundancy exists between abstract and conclusions.

key_strengths: Transparent evaluation of PAROS pre-commercial version at two clinically relevant PI-RADS thresholds with appropriate statistical testing (McNemar's) and CI reporting
Novel quantitative finding that AI systematically underestimates prostate volume by 5.6 mL, with direct implications for PSA density-based risk stratification thresholds
Comprehensive limitations section explicitly addressing biparametric/multiparametric input discrepancy, single-reader design, and population enrichment
PI-QUAL v2 quality exclusion adds methodological rigor by ensuring standardized image quality input
key_concerns: Fundamental design limitation: AI analyzed biparametric MRI while radiologist used full multiparametric sequences, making direct performance comparison inherently unequal and potentially disadvantaging the radiologist
Single expert reader (25 years experience) with no inter-reader analysis prevents evaluation of PAROS performance in supporting less-experienced readers—the primary stated clinical rationale
High csPCa prevalence (63.3%) and very few PI-RADS 1-2 cases due to biopsy-required inclusion make sensitivity/specificity estimates unreliable for screening or low-risk populations
Pre-commercial trial version evaluated—current commercially available PAROS may differ substantially in performance, limiting direct clinical applicability
chief_reviewer.rationale: This single-center diagnostic accuracy study provides useful preliminary comparative data for PAROS against expert radiologist performance, with the important novel measurement calibration finding; Tier 3 is appropriate given incremental contribution and transparent limitations, with minor revisions needed to more prominently address the inherent unfairness of the biparametric vs. multiparametric comparison in the methods section.
